system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 3 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2136-11-28 14:50:00 to 2136-11-30 16:45:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 68-year-old male with a history of quadriplegia, tracheostomy, GJ tube, and chronic Foley catheter was admitted from his nursing home for altered mental status and hypotension. He was found to have hyperkalemia with peaked T waves, acute kidney injury likely due to obstructive uropathy, and hospital-acquired and aspiration pneumonia. He received emergency treatment for hyperkalemia and was started on IV cefepime and linezolid. His Foley catheter was replaced, draining 1.8 liters, and his renal function improved. Sputum culture grew Proteus mirabilis, sensitive to cefepime. Infectious disease recommended completing 8 days of cefepime. The patient refused a PICC line, so he remained hospitalized to complete IV therapy. His warfarin was held due to elevated INR, then restarted at 5 mg daily with bridging enoxaparin due to subtherapeutic levels. Chronic pain from pressure ulcers was managed with increased PRN morphine and palliative care consultation. He was discharged to extended care with instructions to continue antibiotics orally, manage pain, monitor INR, and follow up on electrolytes and vitamin D.
problems: Pneumonitis due to inhalation of food or vomitus
Pneumonia due to other gram-negative bacteria
Delirium due to conditions classified elsewhere
Diabetes with neurological manifestations, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. Johnson. I’m Dr. Lee. You were brought in from your nursing home because you were feeling more tired than usual and your blood work showed a high white blood cell count. Do you understand so far?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I feel weak. Not myself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know you can’t speak much, but thank you for nodding. We’re here to help. Your labs also showed your sodium was high and your kidneys weren’t working as well as usual. We think this might be due to dehydration and possibly a urinary tract infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Back pain… near the sore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we saw your sacral ulcer. It’s stage IV, and we’re concerned about infection. We’ll keep a close eye on it. We replaced your Foley catheter earlier, and it drained about a liter of cloudy urine, which supports the idea of a UTI.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hurts… when I move.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’ve adjusted your pain medications. Since your kidneys weren’t doing well, we lowered your morphine and gabapentin doses temporarily. We’ll increase them back when your kidney function improves.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We started you on an IV antibiotic called meropenem because your urine culture later grew Klebsiella, which is sensitive to this drug. You’ll need to finish a 7-day course.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: IV? At home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go back to extended care, and they’ll continue the IV antibiotic through your existing line. No new PICC needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. Don’t want more tubes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also gave you IV fluids to help your kidneys and correct your high sodium. Your sodium was 146, which can make you feel lethargic. We switched your fluids to D5W to help bring it down safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thirsty… before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that makes sense. Dehydration likely contributed. We’ll make sure your nursing home adjusts your water flushes to prevent this again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your heart rhythm. You’re in normal sinus rhythm, which is good. But your INR was high at 3.8, so we held your warfarin for now. It might be due to recent antibiotics affecting vitamin K.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Blood thinners… safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s safer to pause it until your INR comes down. Your facility will check it and restart warfarin when it’s safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your white blood count has improved—from 14 down to 9.3. That means the antibiotic is working. Your creatinine is also back to normal at 0.3.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Feeling stronger.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. We did an X-ray of your sacrum yesterday because of the back pain and infection concern, but it was hard to get a clear image due to positioning. The wound care team checked and didn’t find signs of bone infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Wound care… what to do?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep turning every few hours, keep heels off the bed, and use a special cushion if you sit up. The dressing will be changed daily with Aquacel Ag and saline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nursing home can do that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they’re trained. We’ll send detailed instructions. Also, we started you on ferrous sulfate for iron deficiency—anemia. Your iron was low, but ferritin was okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Anemia? Again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, chronic issue. But this should help. We also noticed thrush on your tongue, so we’re using nystatin swabs and chlorhexidine rinses. Keep those up at the facility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Mouth feels better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Your diabetes is stable. We used insulin while you were on IV fluids with sugar. You’re back on your usual glargine and sliding scale.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Blood sugars high before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, up to 280. But now they’re around 200, which is better. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today’s the day we discharge you. Your infection has cleared, kidneys are normal, sodium is 143, and you’re feeling better. You’ll finish meropenem over the next few days at the facility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. Ready to go.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll send your warfarin with instructions to restart once your INR is checked. Keep up the wound care, mouth care, and iron pills.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pain meds back to normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, gabapentin and morphine are back to your home doses. Use acetaminophen as needed too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. The facility will follow up on labs and continue palliative care discussions with your family. Let them know if pain or anything else changes.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 68-year-old male with a history of quadriplegia, tracheostomy, GJ tube, and ileostomy was admitted from his nursing home for lethargy and leukocytosis. He was found to have a urinary tract infection caused by Klebsiella pneumoniae, acute kidney injury likely due to dehydration, and hypernatremia. He was treated with IV meropenem and IV fluids, leading to improvement in infection markers and renal function. His supratherapeutic INR led to temporary discontinuation of warfarin. His stage IV sacral ulcer was monitored with no evidence of osteomyelitis, and wound care recommendations were implemented. Iron deficiency anemia was addressed with oral ferrous sulfate, and oral thrush was treated with nystatin and chlorhexidine. He was discharged to extended care to complete his antibiotic course with stable vital signs and resolved symptoms.
